analysis.one_liner: Taxes large employers 100% of the food, housing, and health benefits their workers receive from the government.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge big companies a tax equal to 100% of the federal benefits — food stamps, school meals, Section 8 housing help, and Medicaid — that their own employees receive. The idea is to make low-wage employers, not taxpayers, absorb the cost of their workers' poverty, giving companies a strong reason to raise pay. Companies paying everyone at least $15 an hour, or holding under $100 million in assets, would be exempt. It would also make it illegal for large employers to ask job applicants whether they receive public benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers at very large companies, who would see pressure on their employers to raise wages above benefit-eligibility levels, and taxpayers, who currently foot the bill when billion-dollar companies pay wages too low to live on.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax equal to 100% of the federal food, school meal, housing, and Medicaid benefits received by a large employer's workers, counting part-timers, contractors, and joint employees [S3].

Applies to companies with 500 or more full-time-equivalent employees, with an exemption for employers that pay all workers at least $15 an hour or hold less than $100 million in assets — so the tax hits only the biggest, lowest-paying firms [S3].

Bans large employers from asking job applicants whether they receive federal benefits, backed by lost-wages-plus-equal-liquidated-damages penalties enforced like Fair Labor Standards Act violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Very large companies that pay wages low enough that their workers qualify for food stamps, Medicaid, housing subsidies, or school meals, which would owe a tax equal to those benefits.

drawbacks.text: The tax penalizes employers for their workers' poverty rather than directly raising anyone's pay; a company facing the tax could respond by cutting hours, shifting workers to contractors, or avoiding full-time roles rather than by raising wages [S3].

Employers just under the $15-an-hour line would have an incentive to raise pay to exactly the exemption threshold and no further, and the design taxes benefits the worker needs — a misfired penalty falls on the worker's situation, not just the company's payroll [S3].

Because eligibility depends on household circumstances the employer cannot control (a worker's spouse, children, or other income), the tax could hit companies whose pay practices are not the cause of a given worker's eligibility [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward — make large employers pay for the public cost of their own low wages instead of taxpayers — and the exemption for $15-an-hour firms targets the biggest offenders. The design is blunt, though: it punishes benefit receipt rather than guaranteeing raises, and companies could dodge it by cutting hours or using contractors. It never advanced far enough for those trade-offs to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees the day it was introduced, got zero cosponsors, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on October 23, 2020, less than two weeks before the 2020 election [S1].
It was referred that same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor Committee [S5].
No cosponsor ever signed on, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the bill's history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large low-wage employers avoided a tax tied to their workers' public benefits, and no member beyond the sponsor invested political capital in the idea.

industries.industry: Large low-wage employers (big-box retail, fast food, warehouse and gig-adjacent firms)
industries.note: These firms would owe a tax equal to the SNAP, school lunch, housing, and Medicaid benefits their workers receive — a direct cost unless they raise pay. Their interest in killing the bill ran against workers' interest in higher wages and taxpayers' interest in not subsidizing low pay.

The bill counts independent contractors as employees unless they meet a strict test, closing a route around the tax. Shifting work to contractors would otherwise be a likely way for big employers to avoid it.
